newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil puts bright face on record trade deficit.
newsitem.headline: Brazil puts bright face on record trade deficit.

text.p: Brazil's secretary for economic policy, Jose Roberto Mendonca de Barros, on Thursday struck a positive stance on the economy despite a record monthly trade deficit in October of $1.308 billion.

Blaming the deficit on seasonal demand and the opening of the economy, Mendonca de Barros told reporters sluggish exports would pick up next year when the harvest kicks in around March and when export-boosting measures begin to take effect.

He acknowledged, however, without wishing to make concrete predictions about the trade performance for the rest of the year, that November and December would continue to suffer from the same structural and seasonal factors.

The trade deficit was due to strong imports, he said. "(But) it has more to do with the fact that exports too are growing, but Mendonca de Barros, regarded as the number two man in the Finance Minsitry, said imports could easily expand under economic opening but domestic industry would take longer to react by showing productivity and competitivity gains.

He urged calm, stressing that record foreign direct investment this year of a potential $8.0-9.0 billion would easily help finance an expected 3.0 percent of gross domestic product current account gap for 1996.
And he also noted that the U.S. Federal Reserve's decision to leave U.S. interest rates unchanged made "more tranquil the conditions for financing Brazil's balance of payments".
Mendonca de Barros also pointed out that in the January to October period 1996, imports of durable consumer goods had dropped 34.5 percent while capital goods imports rose 11.8 percent.
"The (import) growth is partly due to demand for productive investment," he said.
Brazil's exports of $4.188 billion in October were composed of 26.7 percent primary goods, 54.15 percent manufactured goods and 18.05 percent semi-manufactured goods.

October's $1.308 billion plunge into the red was the highest monthly trade deficit on record. The second highest monthly gap ever recorded was $1.06 billion in February 1995, when vehicle imports surged dramatically.

Mendonca de Barros said that with the "Plano Real" economic stabilization plan increasingly stamping out inflation, consumer habits had changed. He said seasonal bursts in economic growth at year-end now seemed more dependent on credit than on workers awaiting 13 month salary payments at Christmas time.
Nonchalantly, he assured reporters the government saw no reason to fiddle around with economic policy in order to stem imports and raise the competitivity of exports.

"What we have to evaluate, without minimizing the importance of short-term (results), is the direction everything is taking and I think that without doubt, we will end 1996 having made a lot of progress," he said.
